newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazilians choose mayors in high-tech election.
newsitem.headline: Brazilians choose mayors in high-tech election.

text.p: Brazilians went to the polls on Thursday to elect mayors and councilmen for 5,500 cities in what officials have billed as Latin America's first computerized ballot.
First-round municipal polling kicked off in the morning when voters began punching their candidates' designated numbers into shoe-box sized electronic ballot boxes.

"I had imagined a lot of problems because this is a new way of voting for us. But so far not one thing has gone wrong," Luiz Gonzaga de Freitas, chief supervisor at a busy downtown polling station, said more than an hour into the vote.
Party leaders, worried by news reports suggesting many voters were not aware of their candidate's number, have been emphasizing number over name in the run-up to Thursday's vote.

The three top candidates for Sao Paulo's hotly contested mayoral seat posed for head-to-toe photos on the front cover of the city's leading newspaper which showed them smiling and pointing to a placard carrying their specific number.

Nearly a million candidates across Latin America's largest nation were vying for 5,500 mayoral seats and 60,000 council posts on Thursday, which was declared a national holiday. If necessary, top vote getters will face off in second-round elections next month.

Traffic, housing crime and other local issues have dominated voter concerns, disappointing some opposition leaders who had hoped to turn the vote into a national referendum on President Fernando Henrique's free market reforms.
Some 30 percent of Brazil's 100 million eligible voters were expected to use the electronic ballot boxes, which are a test-run for 1998 presidential elections.
Brazilian election officials said it was the first electronic balloting ever in Latin America and that neighboring countries would monitor the process.

"There are 30 representatives from Argentina, Bolivia, Chile and other Latin American nations here who will accompany us to polling stations to see how this machine performs," said a spokesman at Brazil's Supreme Electoral Tribunal in the capital of Brasilia.
The machines, made by the Brazilian subsidiary of Unisys Corp. of the United States, are expected to deliver results just seven hours after polls close.
Despite a few complaints, voters in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro appeared relatively pleased with the new voting method, saying it was quick and easy to use.

"The vote was easy and much quicker than before. Now I'm going to the beach to play some soccer," said Aldo Grassi Guerrera. One woman, however, complained she had to wait for over an hour to vote due to some confusion over how the new machine worked.
Election officials in Brasilia said they would update preliminary results every half-hour on internet page http://www.tse.gov.br.
